children: By Daisuke Ichikawa / Yomiuri Shimbun Correspondent

DUBLIN — Shingo Ueno, president and CEO of Sumitomo Corp., expressed confidence that the major Japanese trading house will become the industry leader in the aircraft leasing business, a field to which the company is now devoting significant energy.
During an interview with The Yomiuri Shimbun, Ueno said that increasing the company's stock of leasable aircraft to over 2,000 units is within reach.
The following is excerpted from the interview.
The Yomiuri Shimbun: Can you talk about the current state of Sumitomo's aircraft leasing business?

Shingo Ueno: We (indirectly) hold about a one-third stake in (Ireland-based) SMBC Aviation Capital Ltd. through Sumitomo Mitsui Finance and Leasing Co., which we co-own with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group Inc. This year, we joined with SMBC Aviation Capital and other partners to acquire the U.S.-based aircraft leasing firm Air Lease Corp. (now Sumisho Air Lease Corp.).
Yomiuri: What is the current business environment surrounding aircraft leasing?

Ueno: Demand for aircraft is steadily increasing. The current fleet stands at about 35,000 units, but it is projected to grow to between 50,000 and 55,000 in the next 20 years. Airlines are increasingly moving away from owning aircraft, which are heavy assets, opting instead to lease them, improving their asset efficiency.

Furthermore, new aircraft are slow to enter the market. This supply scarcity makes it possible for us to sell our aircraft to airlines looking for used options. As shown in this example, we operate on a variety of business models.
Yomiuri: The number of aircraft is increasing, but what about the proportion of leased aircraft compared to those owned by airlines? Is that also rising?

Ueno: Currently, leased aircraft account for roughly half of the about 35,000 planes that exist (in the world). Assuming the fleet reaches 50,000 in 20 years, this 50% threshold represents a bare minimum that will likely be surpassed.

Yomiuri: With the acquisition of Air Lease, Sumitomo Corp. became the world's second largest company in the aircraft leasing market in terms of fleet size. Do you aim to expand your fleet to make yourself No. 1?

Ueno: Our fleet stands at 1,903 units (including order backlog, as of July 2026). The top company has 2,000 aircraft, so we're closing in on them. Exceeding the 2,000-aircraft mark is a very achievable goal.
Yomiuri: What has been the impact of the recent depreciation of the yen against the dollar in the foreign exchange market?

Ueno: We project an exchange rate of 150 yen to the dollar for the current fiscal year, so if the yen weakens by 1 yen to the dollar, our net profit increases by 2 billion yen, and simple math shows a 10-yen depreciation would result in a 20-billion-yen gain. However, a weaker yen is not entirely cause for celebration. For instance, it significantly increases the costs to import construction materials and equipment. Our preference is for a stable exchange rate, rather than seeing the yen fluctuate in either direction. A stable rate allows us to plan long-term projects and forecast future earnings.
Yomiuri: How about the impact of rising interest rates?
Ueno: Rising interest rates increase financing costs, but since we generally pass those costs on through sales prices, the impact isn't that significant.
Yomiuri: What are your plans for improving your stock price and returning value to shareholders, and what is your target market capitalization?

Ueno: We will make efforts to improve our price-to-book ratio (PBR) so that our stock price will continue rising. The PBR equals the price-to-earnings ratio multiplied by the return on equity (ROE), so we will focus on boosting ROE. We have set a target of posting an annual ROE of at least 12% in our (current) medium-term business plan. The figure was 12.9% last fiscal year, and we aim to raise it further this fiscal year. Regarding shareholder returns, we have set a target of achieving a total payout ratio of at least 40%, which we aim to meet through a combination of dividends and share buybacks.
